title: The Black Death
hook: plague sweeps Europe; some priests flee, others stay to bury and bless

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rublev's three visitors at the table, with a gap at the front. Your line was the open place. Who did you leave room for? Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

"Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness." That's a line from Psalm ninety-one in the King James Bible, a psalm about trusting God when danger is everywhere. In the Middle Ages, a pestilence walked through the towns of Europe in broad daylight. A sickness that came fast, with fever and swellings. Whole households emptied. Markets closed. Graveyards filled, and then there wasn't room. People ran from the cities if they could. And in town after town the same question arrived at the church door: who will come to the sick? Who will hear their last words, and bury them? Today: the Black Death.

We don't have to guess how hard it was. People wrote it down while it was happening, and the writers of the time describe priests, doctors and neighbors facing a choice. Some fled. It's hard to blame them; the sickness spread from person to person, and staying could mean dying. But some stayed. Priests went into houses where the sick lay, to hear confession, to anoint, to give the last communion. Monks and nuns nursed people they didn't know. Ordinary townspeople carried the dead to be buried when no family was left to do it. Some of those who stayed caught the sickness and died themselves. Why stay? The answer goes back to the scene we met with Elizabeth of Hungary, the sheep and the goats in the Gospel of Matthew, where the king also says to the righteous, in the King James Bible: "I was sick, and ye visited me". They ask when they ever did that, and he tells them that whatever they did for the least of these, they did for him. Catholic tradition gathered acts like these into a list called the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, and also burying the dead, which comes from the book of Tobit. Protestant churches place Tobit outside their canon of scripture, but they kept the same command to visit the sick from Matthew. So the plague years hold two stories side by side. One is terror, and flight, and blame, and real cruelty toward people treated as outsiders. The other is quieter, and shorter to tell. Some stayed.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the people who stay with the sick. Let them come to mind one by one. A nurse finishing a night shift. A doctor making one more call. Someone cleaning a hospital room. A chaplain at a bedside. A family member who has given up sleep to sit with someone they love. If you know one of them by name, let that face come. If you pray, you can pray for them, for strength and for rest. If you don't, just hold them in your thoughts, and let gratitude sit there with them. The bell holds the time.
The Black Death. The plague that swept through Europe in the Middle Ages, when some fled the sick, and some stayed to nurse, bless and bury them.
Your line: some stayed. Today, thank one person whose work keeps them near the sick, a nurse, a caregiver, a friend sitting at a bedside, out loud or in a short note. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians remember the plague years when they pray for the sick and for those who care for them, and Catholic Christians still teach visiting the sick and burying the dead among the works of mercy.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'a third of Europe dies' was cut; no death toll, date or percentage is stated. The hook field was reworded accordingly; the index itself is unchanged.
'Some of those who stayed caught the sickness and died themselves' and 'often killed within days' are general history from chronicles of the time, not a cited text here. Confirm or soften.

'Real cruelty toward people treated as outsiders' alludes to the massacres of Jewish communities blamed for the plague; kept unnamed and brief so it is not used as drama. Keeper may prefer to name it plainly or cut it.
Works of mercy: the seven corporal works, with burying the dead drawn from Tobit; confirm the Orthodox framing as well as the Catholic one.
The name 'Black Death' is later than the plague itself; deliberately not discussed (claims rule on etymology).
Editor: cut the unsourced 'often killed within days' and changed 'in every town' to 'in town after town'.

Editor (second pass): the works of mercy are now credited to Catholic tradition only (the Orthodox framing was unconfirmed), and Matthew 25 is tied back to Elizabeth of Hungary (day 820), which used the same scene, so it reads as a link rather than a repeat.

Auditor: replaced the garbled 'the middle centuries' with 'the Middle Ages' (hook and word); 'don't count Tobit as scripture' is now 'place Tobit outside their canon', since Lutheran and Anglican Bibles still print the Apocrypha for reading.
